opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of the hardest problems, honestly, because it's really about reading intent, and users don't always state their intent explicitly. Someone might say "write me a blog post about X," and do they want a quick answer in chat, or do they want a document they'll iterate on, edit, and come back to? Those are very different experiences.

The way we approached it was to think about what the user is trying to *do*, not just what they're asking for. If it's something substantial they'll probably want to refine, like a long piece of writing or a chunk of code they'll edit, that's a good signal for Canvas. If it's a quick factual question or a short back-and-forth, opening a side panel is jarring and gets in the way.

The failure modes cut both ways. If you over-trigger, it feels annoying and presumptuous, like the model is taking over your screen. If you under-trigger, people who'd benefit from the collaborative editing never discover it. So a lot of the work was calibrating that decision boundary, and much of it came down to building good evals and, in our case, a lot of synthetic data to teach the model when to invoke the tool and when not to.

It also generalizes beyond Canvas. As models get more tools, like search, code execution, and different interfaces, the meta-skill is "which affordance fits this moment?" That's really a model behavior question, not just a product one. Ideally the user shouldn't have to think about it. The model should just pick the right medium, and if it gets it wrong, it should be very easy to redirect.

r001.rationale: The response calls judging user intent about whether to use Canvas “one of the hardest problems” and discusses choosing Canvas versus other tools. That clearly communicates the criterion.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually one of the hardest problems, and I think people underestimate it. When we launched Canvas, the core question was: when should the model decide to open a canvas versus just respond in chat? And it sounds simple, but user intent is really ambiguous.

Like, if someone says "write me a short poem," do they want that in a canvas or in the chat? Probably chat, right? It's short, they want to read it inline. But if they say "help me draft an essay for my college application," that's clearly something they'll iterate on, so a canvas makes sense. The hard part is everything in between.

So the way we approached it was, we had to define what the triggering behavior should be, and then train the model against that. We built evals with human raters, we wrote out these decision boundaries pretty carefully, and we found the model was initially over-triggering a lot. It would open a canvas for things like a quick Q&A answer, and that's really annoying as a user, because it disrupts the flow. Over-triggering is actually worse than under-triggering, I think, because it feels like the tool is imposing itself on you.

And it becomes more complicated when you have multiple tools. Canvas is one, but there's also browsing, code interpreter, image generation, and the model has to pick. So it's really a routing problem on top of the core capability. We did a lot of work on, I guess you'd call it tool-calling calibration, where the model learns to be conservative and only use a tool when it genuinely adds value.

Something I believe strongly is that this should also be learned from implicit feedback over time. If a user keeps closing the canvas or keeps asking to just put it in chat, the model should adapt. We're not fully there yet, but that's the direction. The ideal is that the model builds up a sense of how you work and what you prefer, rather than applying one rule to everyone.

r001.rationale: The response calls deciding when to open Canvas one of the hardest problems and describes choosing among Canvas and other tools as a routing problem.

astra-6.text: I think the challenge is that users usually express what they want to accomplish, rather than which tool they want to use. If someone says, “Help me write this,” do they want a quick draft in the chat, or do they want a document they can keep editing in Canvas? Both are reasonable interpretations. So the model has to infer that from the context and the kind of collaboration the user seems to want. And then it needs to be easy to redirect, because you’re not always going to get that inference right.

r001.rationale: The response describes inferring whether a user wants Canvas or another tool as a challenge, but does not say it is one of the hardest remaining problems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s fundamentally an intent problem. When someone asks you to write something, do they want a quick answer in the chat, or do they want a document they can keep editing? They don’t necessarily tell you explicitly. You have to infer that from the task and the conversation.

And there are really two decisions: whether to use a tool at all, and then which tool makes sense. With Canvas, the question is whether having a separate workspace will help the user iterate. You want the model to recognize that opportunity without making the interaction feel unpredictable or adding friction to a simple request.

r001.rationale: The response describes inferring user intent as a challenge, but does not identify it as one of the hardest remaining problems.
